clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive dystrophy caused by mutations in CYP4V2, a fatty-acid metabolism gene, with relatively high prevalence in East Asian populations
Characterised by numerous glistening yellow-white crystalline deposits scattered throughout the posterior pole, with retinal pigment epithelium and choriocapillaris atrophy
Crystals may also be seen at the corneoscleral limbus, and lipid crystalline inclusions can be found in circulating lymphocytes and other cells
Patients present in early adulthood with declining acuity, nyctalopia and progressive visual field constriction
Electroretinography deteriorates over time and can show a cone-rod or rod-cone pattern depending on stage
Optical coherence tomography demonstrates hyper-reflective crystalline dots with progressive outer retinal, retinal pigment epithelium and choroidal thinning
Management is supportive with genetic counselling and low-vision rehabilitation, with gene-directed therapy under investigation
reference.pathophysiology: Bietti crystalline dystrophy results from biallelic mutations in CYP4V2, which encodes a cytochrome P450 enzyme involved in fatty-acid and corticosteroid metabolism. Impaired lipid processing leads to accumulation of crystalline lipid deposits within the retina, retinal pigment epithelium and other tissues, with secondary degeneration of photoreceptors, retinal pigment epithelium and the underlying choriocapillaris. Progressive atrophy of the outer retina and choroid produces the characteristic slowly advancing chorioretinal degeneration and visual decline.
additionalDifferentials: Drug-induced crystalline retinopathy (for example tamoxifen, canthaxanthin)
Oxalosis and other metabolic crystalline retinopathies
Talc retinopathy from intravenous drug use
Retinitis pigmentosa and other rod-cone dystrophies
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination documenting posterior pole crystalline deposits and atrophy
Optical coherence tomography for hyper-reflective crystals and outer retinal/choroidal thinning
Fundus autofluorescence to map retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptor loss
Full-field electroretinography to assess and monitor cone and rod function
Molecular genetic testing for CYP4V2 mutations
redFlags: Progressive constriction of visual fields and night blindness indicating advancing degeneration
Rapid central acuity loss requiring reassessment and counselling
Systemic or drug history suggesting a treatable acquired crystalline retinopathy instead
Affected siblings who warrant screening given recessive inheritance
reference.prognosis: The disorder is progressive, with gradual decline in acuity and visual field over decades and eventual severe visual impairment in many patients, though the rate is variable.
pitfalls: Mistaking the crystalline deposits for a benign incidental finding or a drug-induced retinopathy without a full history
Assuming limbal crystals are always present, as they may be subtle or absent
Failing to counsel about recessive inheritance and sibling risk
Attributing early symptoms to refractive error rather than a retinal dystrophy
